audit.comment: C’s larger learning rate accelerated boundary learning within 256 updates; I overestimated RMSprop instability and overweighted Adam’s β₂ difference. On an independent 1.5-turn spiral with the exact architecture and budget, controlled replication produced CE A=0.0222, B=0.0374, C=0.00247. RMSprop at 0.001 gave 0.00966, while Adam at 0.003 gave 0.000995: learning rate is a major cause, not universal RMSprop superiority. K1005 warned against letting β₂ override learning-rate differences; K1009 also supported prioritizing optimization progress. I failed to apply those warnings. K1040’s longer-budget β₂ observation was not decisive here.

The main missed mechanism was optimizer progress, not LayerNorm count. At only 256×16 updates, AdamW at 0.003 (D) is far more likely to escape the near-chance plateau than 0.001 recipes, while Adagrad’s accumulator makes B’s nominal 0.003 less effective. A’s Adam 0.001/GELU recipe edges C’s AdamW 0.001/leaky-ReLU recipe in this short-budget regime. E’s 3e-5 Adam is effectively frozen. K1020 misled me by elevating LN count within architecture-matched comparisons; K1040 did not justify treating AdamW as universally superior.

I treated this separable one-turn problem as necessarily undertrained. The missed distinction is boundary learning versus subsequent confidence optimization: A’s AdamW with β₂=0.95 can forget early large gradients and continue increasing margins, despite its small nominal learning rate. B’s β₂=0.999 retains those gradients much longer, and coupled decay can limit confidence. C’s Adagrad likewise retains accumulated gradients. These are supported explanations, not isolated causes on this split. No KB was consulted originally. K1001’s “every task is under-trained” premise would reinforce the mistake; K1005’s optimizer-knob exception and K1040 point toward the confidence-tail regime, although K1040’s tested decay is larger than B’s. Backtests support only a provisional, narrow rule.

B won with the shared GELU architecture and learning rate, consistent with shorter second-moment memory helping optimization of the harder 2.5-turn spiral within 1024 steps. C’s tiny Adagrad learning rate makes it an underfitting candidate. K1040 usefully identifies the boundary of its AdamW advantage: coupled Adam decay hurts most when simpler spirals are already fit to very low CE, whereas harder, under-trained spirals may favor faster adaptation. Its strong AdamW preference should not be extrapolated to this instance. This result supports that scope distinction, but does not isolate β₂ from coupled versus decoupled decay.

The missed factor was RMSprop’s short-budget acceleration, not model capacity: D and E have identical networks. Default RMSprop starts its uncorrected squared-gradient accumulator at zero, producing larger initial normalized updates than bias-corrected AdamW; its lack of momentum also changes adaptation as the spiral features develop. My preference for AdamW’s smoother optimization was unsupported here. A controlled 1.5-turn, shallow GELU/LayerNorm experiment confirmed RMSprop’s advantage at 256 steps: CE 0.394 versus AdamW’s 0.511 at lr=0.003. The retrieved KB claims K1032, K1040, and K1020 did not establish this optimizer ordering and did not cause the error.

The decisive axis was optimizer progress within 1024 steps: AdamW at 1e-3 beat the 1e-4 variants, while SGD at 3e-4 lagged. Among the low-rate adaptive candidates, β2=0.999 beat 0.95, and coupled Adam decay placed D below its AdamW near-twin C. K1005 supported prioritizing learning rate over secondary knobs. K1040 was directionally consistent with both the low-rate β2 ordering and the coupled-decay penalty, but its measured regime differs from this deeper, layer-normalized, two-turn case; this result alone does not establish an extension of that claim.

A’s moderate-rate recipe beat B’s tenfold-higher rate and decay; C’s smaller rate provided insufficient progress. The plausible missed mechanism is late-stage refinement: larger displacement need not improve cross-entropy after learning an easy spiral boundary. However, the revealed winner cannot distinguish learning-rate instability from coupled-decay effects. K1001 and K1004 misled by treating this regime as under-trained and high rates as safe; K1005/K1040 did not establish safety at decay 1e-4. Backtesting found higher rates winning 19/19 architecture-matched history comparisons and 4/4 matched lab pairs. All lab spiral runs used 256 steps, not 2048. Thus no general ceiling or revised decay threshold is sufficiently tested to propose.
